Newborn Care

Is your baby overheating? Signs, cooling and prevention

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A baby can get too hot in summer sunshine or under winter layers. Their temperature, feeding and behaviour all matter. Simple changes may improve comfort, but serious heat illness and a young infant’s fever need prompt care.

Overheating can happen in any season

A picnic, a warm bedroom or a journey in the car can expose a baby to more heat than they can comfortably manage. Babies cannot explain that they feel too hot or move themselves to a cooler place. They depend on an adult to notice their surroundings, clothing and behaviour.

Summer weather is an obvious concern, but thick layers and heated rooms can also cause overheating in winter. Check the baby, not just the season. A cool day outside does not mean that a baby needs heavy clothing in a warm house or car.

Know when to call for emergency help

Call your local emergency number if a baby exposed to heat is difficult to wake, unresponsive, having a seizure, struggling to breathe or behaving very abnormally. Marked drowsiness, weakness or confusion with a very hot body can signal serious heat illness. Do not wait for a particular thermometer number before seeking help.

Begin cooling while help is being arranged: move out of the heat, remove excess clothing and gently cool the skin with cool water. Follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. Never force a drink into a baby who is too sleepy to feed or swallow safely. Stay with them and tell the dispatcher immediately if breathing changes.

Look for a pattern of warning signs

An overheated baby may feel unusually hot over the chest or back, have flushed skin, sweaty hair or damp clothing, or become restless and irritable. Other concerning changes include a fast heartbeat or breathing, vomiting, unusual tiredness, weakness and reduced responsiveness. A young infant’s behaviour and feeding may tell you more than a visible skin change.

Redness is less easy to see on some skin tones, and sweating is not a reliable rule-out test. A baby can be dangerously hot without looking sweaty. Check the chest or back of the neck rather than relying on cool hands or feet, and pay attention to whether your baby is responding as usual.

Measure temperature without assuming the cause

Normal body temperature varies with the baby, time of day and measurement method. A figure such as 36.4°C is an approximate reference, not the single normal reading every baby should have. Use an age-appropriate digital thermometer as instructed; measurements from different body sites are not interchangeable.

A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment. Do not dismiss this as warm weather or wait to see whether feeding fixes it. Environmental overheating and a fever from illness have different causes, and a baby can have an infection even after spending time somewhere hot. Mention recent heat exposure and how you measured the temperature.

Make the sleeping room comfortable

Use a room thermometer as a guide and check how your baby feels. The UK Lullaby Trust recommends a sleeping-room range of 16–20°C, while practical advice can vary with climate and local guidance. A different range such as 20–22°C, or a precise upper limit of 23.8°C, should not be treated as a universal boundary between safe and unsafe sleep.

Adjust clothing and room conditions together. A temperature display on a baby monitor is not automatically more accurate than a separate room thermometer, and a monitor cannot replace checking the baby. If one room is very warm, consider another cooler room with a suitable safe sleep space.

Reduce heat indoors during summer

Close curtains or blinds before strong sun heats the room, especially around a sunny window. Ventilate when outdoor air is cooler and it is safe to open a window. A fan can help move air, but keep it and its cord safely out of reach and avoid aiming it directly at the baby.

If your home stays uncomfortably hot, plan where you can go to cool down: an air-conditioned library, a shopping centre or an accessible community cooling space may help. Think ahead about transport, feeding and a place for safe sleep. In extreme conditions, moving to a cooler environment is more useful than continuing to add small comfort measures in a very hot room.

Plan outings around shade and cooler hours

Choose cooler parts of the day for a walk or outing and use local heat and UV advice rather than a fixed clock rule for every country. Keep young babies out of direct sun. Light, breathable clothing and a suitable pram sunshade can help, but a blanket over the pram can trap heat and obstruct airflow.

Check frequently during pool trips, picnics and travel, including when a baby seems to be sleeping peacefully. Never leave a baby alone in a parked car, even on a mild day, even briefly and even with a window open. A shaded parking place is not a reliable protection as the sun and temperature change.

Avoid overbundling in winter

Use layers that you can remove as the surroundings warm up. The familiar suggestion of roughly one extra light layer compared with a comfortably dressed adult is a starting point, not a reason to keep adding blankets regardless of the baby’s temperature. Keep sleep spaces away from radiators, heating vents, portable heaters and fireplaces.

Bulky coats and snowsuits should not sit beneath a car-seat harness because compression can leave the harness too loose in a crash. Use thin layers and follow the seat instructions. Any covering used over a secured harness should stay clear of the face, and extra coverings should come off as the car warms. Recheck the baby after moving between outdoors, the car and home.

Keep safe sleep precautions in warm and cold weather

Overheating is associated with an increased risk of sudden infant death syndrome, but it is not the only factor and does not explain every death. Put a baby on their back on a firm, flat, level sleep surface with a fitted sheet. Keep pillows, loose blankets, soft toys and other soft items out of the sleep space.

Choose sleep clothing suited to the conditions and keep the head uncovered indoors. Do not use extra bedding to compensate for hands that feel cooler than the chest. A cooler room or a monitoring device does not make an otherwise unsafe sleep arrangement safe.

Cool an alert baby who feels too warm

Move to a cooler place, take off unnecessary layers and replace wet, heavy clothing with something light if needed. For environmental overheating, a cool damp cloth or gentle cooling with water can help. Keep watching the baby’s responsiveness and breathing rather than treating cooling as a task you can finish and leave.

This is different from routinely sponging a baby with an infection-related fever, which is not recommended. Do not use ice directly on the skin or give fever medicine as a substitute for cooling serious heat illness. Seek medical advice promptly if symptoms persist, feeding falls or you are unsure what is causing the temperature. Do not apply an adult “wait 30 minutes” rule to a sick young infant.

Offer feeds appropriate for the baby’s age

An alert baby who can feed safely may want breastfeeds more often in hot weather. For a baby using formula, keep offering correctly prepared feeds; never dilute formula to provide extra water. Milk should not be displaced by large amounts of water.

Guidance on small additional water feeds for formula-fed infants under 6 months differs between countries. Ask a local child-health professional what is appropriate rather than improvising. Exclusively breastfed babies usually meet their fluid needs through additional breastfeeds. From around 6 months, when complementary foods begin, small drinks of water can accompany meals while breast milk or formula remains important.

Notice dehydration and heat rash

Fewer wet nappies than usual, dry mouth, fewer tears when crying, poor feeding and unusual sleepiness can indicate dehydration. The change from your baby’s usual pattern matters. A baby who cannot keep feeds down or is becoming less responsive needs prompt assessment, not repeated attempts to push in more fluid.

Heat rash produces small raised spots and a prickly or irritated feeling, often where heat and sweat collect, such as around the neck or covered skin. Spots may look red, grey or pale depending on skin tone. Keep the skin cool and clothing light, but do not assume every nappy-area rash is heat rash. Get advice if the rash worries you, persists or occurs with illness.

Distinguish discomfort from serious heat illness

Being too warm may disrupt sleep and make a baby unsettled. Heat exhaustion can also involve vomiting, weakness, sweating or clammy skin and a raised temperature. Heatstroke is a medical emergency, particularly when consciousness, behaviour or breathing changes. These conditions cannot be reliably separated at home by checking one symptom.

A baby who is persistently inconsolable, repeatedly vomiting, feeding poorly or still unusually hot after moving into a cooler environment needs urgent advice. If they are difficult to wake, have a seizure or develop breathing difficulty, call emergency services. Tell the clinician the baby’s age, exposure, temperature, wet-nappy pattern and steps already taken.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Overheating prevention includes the room, clothing, travel and safe sleep environment.

Heat illness and infection-related fever need different responses; an unwell infant should not be judged by temperature alone.

How BeMama can help

Before an outing or bedtime, check the room, clothing, feed access and a plan for moving somewhere cooler.

When to seek help

Call emergency services for difficulty waking, seizures or breathing difficulty after heat exposure. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check the chest or back of the neck and the baby’s behaviour.
  • Avoid overbundling in winter as well as direct heat in summer.
  • Continue appropriate milk feeds and never dilute formula.
  • Use a clear, firm, flat sleep space in every season.
  • Do not delay help for an unusually sleepy or poorly feeding baby.

Frequently asked questions

Can a baby overheat in winter?

Yes. A heated room or car combined with thick clothing and extra blankets can make a baby too hot.

Does a baby have to sweat to be overheating?

No. Lack of sweat does not exclude dangerous heat illness; responsiveness, breathing and overall condition matter.

Is 36.4°C the only normal temperature?

No. Normal readings vary, including with the method used. An unwell baby needs assessment even when a reading is not dramatically high.

What if my baby is under 3 months and reaches 38°C?

Seek urgent medical assessment. Do not assume warm weather is the only cause or wait for cooling to rule out infection.

Does every bedroom have to be exactly 20°C?

No single number guarantees safety. Follow local sleep guidance, adjust clothing and check your baby. The Lullaby Trust recommends a range of 16–20°C.

Can I use a fan?

You can use one to help circulate room air, positioned safely out of reach and away from directly blowing on the baby. Seek a cooler place if the room remains very hot.

Should I give extra water to a young baby?

Continue milk feeds. Exclusively breastfed babies usually need more breastfeeds, and local guidance varies for formula-fed babies under 6 months. Ask a child-health professional and never dilute formula.

Is a heat rash the same as heatstroke?

No. Heat rash is a skin condition; heatstroke is a life-threatening illness. A rash does not tell you how well the rest of the baby is coping.

Can fever medicine treat overheating?

It does not replace cooling and urgent assessment for serious heat illness. Do not delay care to see whether medicine works.

Should I wait 30 minutes before asking for help?

Not when a young baby is unwell or there are warning signs. Difficulty waking, seizures or breathing problems require emergency help immediately.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
